title: Anonymous LLC states: which states show LLC member names
summary: Anonymous LLC states: what each state's formation filing and annual report name, in a 51-row table, and how Sixtyfour researches who is behind an LLC.
body_markdown:
No state labels an LLC anonymous, but in some the public filings name no member or manager at all. Reading each state's own forms in November 2026, we found twelve where neither the formation filing nor the annual report asks for one: Alabama, Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Maryland, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Virginia and Wyoming. Several of them still name the organiser or the person who signed, who need not be a member.


A few ask for at least some members by name whoever runs the LLC. Alaska's biennial report lists members who own 5 percent or more, Kansas's information report lists members with 5 percent or more of the capital, Arizona's articles list the members of a member-managed LLC and the members owning 20 percent or more of a manager-managed one, and the District of Columbia asks for each member or manager with more than 10 percent of the ownership or control. Many other states ask for the managers, or for at least one member or manager, which can mean a manager is named and no owner is.


In many states the public filings do not name an LLC's members, so the state's record alone may not show who owns it. Members and the people acting for them still appear in other records: a deed or mortgage the LLC signed, a financing statement, a court case, a filing in another state where the LLC is registered, or the company's own website and press. Rhode Island, for example, says it "does not keep a record of who owns any registered business".


Not necessarily. The registered agent receives legal papers for the LLC, and Colorado's filing help notes that the agent "isn't necessarily an owner or director". Many LLCs use a commercial agent that serves many companies, so an agent's name or address links nothing on its own.


Check every state where the LLC is registered to do business, because each keeps its own filings and some ask for managers or members. Then search the county recorder, financing statements and court records under the LLC's name, and read who signed for it. The company's own website, press coverage and the profiles of people who say they run it fill in the rest, and each name stays a lead until a second, independent record agrees.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes an LLC's name or website and returns the fields you ask for, such as its managers and members, its parent company and the people who run it, each with the URL it was read on. A research plan can tell it to follow a parent company until it reaches a person, a field it could not establish comes back empty, and a person on your team decides.
